implementation_notes: Swift packages the pattern into the language: withTaskGroup is the master, group.addTask creates identical child tasks (@Sendable closures, so the compiler rejects most shared-mutable-state escapes), and the group's lifetime is the join - the API does not return until every child has completed, even if the body returns early. Partial results are collected as they complete with for await partial in group (completion order, good for dynamic aggregation) or with next()/waitForAll(); async let covers a fixed small set. Cancellation is cooperative and explicit: cancelAll() only signals, children must check Task.checkCancellation. Before Swift 5.5 the same structure was DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform, which runs the block once per iteration and returns only after all iterations complete; OperationQueue with maxConcurrentOperationCount is the heavier pre-concurrency option.
pitfalls: The group always awaits its children: an early return still waits for all of them, so cancelAll() plus cooperative cancellation checks are required to stop useless work.
Child closures are @Sendable and run outside any actor: capturing mutable class state either fails to compile or races (move it behind an actor).
Cancellation never interrupts synchronous work - a blocking call keeps running unless it is moved off the task or checks Task.isCancelled.
Adding unbounded tasks (one per input element) over a huge collection floods the cooperative pool; batch, or use addTaskUnlessCancelled with a window.
